intro: If you own minerals under a farm or wooded parcel near South Boardman, chances are somebody leased it during the Antrim boom decades ago, a well went in, and the royalty checks have been trickling in on autopilot ever since — smaller every few years, but still showing up. Most folks never think about that interest until a life event forces the question: a divorce, an estate to settle, a stack of medical bills. That's usually when people start Googling what the thing is even worth.

We buy mineral and royalty interests in and around South Boardman. We're not appraisers and we're not your attorney — we're a straight buyer who'll pull your production history and give you a number tied to what the well is actually doing, not a guess.

sections.heading: The Antrim Play Around South Boardman
paragraphs: South Boardman sits inside the Antrim Shale core, the same Devonian black shale trend that runs through most of Kalkaska County. These are shallow wells, generally under 2,000 feet, producing biogenic gas along with a fair amount of formation water that has to be handled and disposed of — that water handling cost is one reason Antrim economics run differently than a conventional oil well.

Wells here typically peaked early and have been on a long, gentle decline for years. If yours was one of the ones drilled in the late 1980s or early '90s rush, it's likely well past its productive prime and into the low, flat tail that can still run for a long while yet, just at reduced volumes.

sections.heading: What a Buyer Actually Looks At
paragraphs: When we look at a South Boardman interest, we're not eyeballing the county and quoting a flat number. We pull actual monthly production or your check history, figure out where the well sits on its decline curve, and price the remaining stream against current gas pricing and the realistic time the well has left. That's the honest way to do it. It's also why any offer that arrives in your mailbox with a dollar figure already printed on it, before anyone's looked at your actual production, deserves a second look before you sign.

Small checks aren't a sign of a worthless interest — sometimes they're the sign of a well that's stabilized and will keep paying modestly for a long stretch, which has its own kind of value to a buyer thinking long-term.

sections.heading: Ownership Gets Tangled Out Here Too
paragraphs: Kalkaska County has plenty of mineral interests that never got cleanly passed down — split among siblings, tied up in an estate that was never formally probated, or still sitting under a name that's been dead for twenty years. If that's your situation, it doesn't disqualify you from selling, it just means there's a step or two of paperwork to clear at the register of deeds and probate court before a closing can happen.
We deal with this constantly. Tell us what you've got, even if the deed's a mess, and we'll tell you honestly what it'll take to get it sale-ready.

faqs.question: My well near South Boardman barely pays anymore. Is it worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. A stable low-volume well still represents years of remaining cash flow to a buyer, even if the monthly check looks small to you. We'll run the actual numbers.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer to sell my interest?
faqs.answer: Not always, but if your ownership is tangled through an estate or unprobated will, an attorney can speed things up. We'll flag it if we see that's the case.

faqs.question: How fast can this close?
faqs.answer: Once we have your division order or check stub and the title's clear, most South Boardman deals can close in a few weeks.
